World Models Are Here...So 
What Do They Mean for U, 
RBLX, TTWO and APP? 
World models like GOOGL's Genie are here, raising concerns 
about game industry disruption. We think the long term risk is 
real, but also see key hurdles for world models that give 
incumbents time to respond. We outline scenarios for what 
could come next and implications for U, RBLX, TTWO, and APP.

Industry View
Attractive
GOOGL's Genie 3 World Model Is Here and Disruption Fears Are Rising: On 1/29, 
GOOGL announced it was rolling out its Genie 3 world model for subscribers to 
test. This hands-on experience raised concerns that world models could disrupt how 
video games are produced, impacting industry leaders including U (-24% on 1/30), 
APP (-17%), RBLX (-13%), and TTWO (-7%). As we noted in 10 Debates to Shape the 
Sector in '26, we see the impact of world models as a key debate for the game 
industry this year. 
Looking Ahead, We See Two Scenarios For Today's Game Industry Leaders: Adapt 
or Be Replaced... We see two main scenarios for today's game industry leaders over 
the longer term (see Exhibit 1 ): Scenario 1, where incumbents adapt their tools 
and frameworks to use new AI technology; or Scenario 2, where incumbents are 
replaced or severely disrupted by new AI technology. Scenario 1 assumes that tools 
like U's Engine and Roblox Studio deploy AI tools to automate manual processes like 
coding and 3D asset creation. The structure of traditional game engines would 
remain, but automation would increasingly take center stage.

Key Takeaways
 GOOGL’s Genie 3 launch has sparked fears that world models could disrupt how 
video games are produced, with negative implications for many incumbent firms
Long term, incumbents face two paths: adapt existing tools and frameworks to 
integrate AI or risk being disrupted by these new technologies 
That said, world models face key hurdles including determinism, memory, and 
updates that we think could make it simpler to deploy AI within existing 
frameworks
Short
term constraints (cost, speed, stability) give incumbents time to respond, 
but long
term AI disruption risk remains real
In our view: APP is low risk/arguably not exposed; U is exposed but adapting; 
RBLX is also exposed but highly defensible; TTWO has exposure but protected by 
IP.

Exhibit 1:
We see two main scenarios for how AI tools could be used to 
automate video game production in the coming years: Scenario 1 where 
incumbents adapt their tools and frameworks to use new AI technology; and 
Scenario 2, where incumbents are replaced or severely disrupted by new AI 
technology.
Source: Company Data, Morgan Stanley Research
...But Replacing Existing Game Tech Could Be Harder Than it Appears at First 
Glance: Scenario 2 is the simpler option, since world models can already generate 
playable, video game-like worlds from natural language prompts alone. But we see 
a number challenges that may slow or prevent world models from replacing (as 
opposed to augmenting) existing game technology. Some of these challenges, like 
compute speed and cost to operate, have clear paths to solutions and will likely be 
solved in the near term. Others, including meta systems and latency, create larger 
roadblocks that will require further research and investment to clear, but may 
eventually be solved. However, certain major issues like determinism, memory, 
and updates could ultimately be difficult to solve within the context of a world 
model.
Exhibit 2:
Several roadblocks prevent world models from generating complete 
and playable games today (i.e. Scenario 2), but some of them pose significant 
long-term hurdles.
Source: Company Data, Morgan Stanley Research
 It Remains Unclear Whether Certain Major Challenges Are Solvable, Including A 
Lack of Determinism and Persistent Memory: For example, today's world models 
are probabilistic, not deterministic, meaning they lack a single "source of truth" to 
govern interactions between multiple players. That means a world model running 
the same game for multiple players might show objects at slightly different 
locations or moving at different speeds. That is because at their core, these models 
are predicting where an object likely sits, as opposed to referencing an objective 
data point. Memory presents similar structural challenges, as world models are not

Morgan Stanley Research
3
designed to store large amounts of information about the game-state in a 
persistent way. A process to update live instances also remains unknown. So while 
it might be possible to re-engineer solutions to these issues over time, we question 
whether deploying generative AI is actually simpler within existing frameworks. 
In our view, that makes Scenario 1 the likelier path, i.e. taking today's games engines 
and using world models (and other AI tools) to automate the game production 
process while leveraging existing solutions to these challenges. 
Exhibit 3:
We see a lack of determinism, constraints on memory, and issues with 
updates as key unsolved roadblocks to using world models to build games at 
scale. We question whether it is simpler to re-engineer solutions to these (and 
other) issues within a world model, or to use AI to automate game creation within 
existing engine architecture.
Source: Company Data, Morgan Stanley Research

Source: Company Data, Morgan Stanley Research
Short-Term Constraints on World Models Create Time for Incumbents to 
Respond, But the Long Term Threat is Real: While demos of Genie 3 already 
generate high-fidelity interactive worlds in seconds based on user prompts (see 
here), this is still an early test. As mentioned above, we believe these world models 
face short-term constraints in their speed, stability, and cost. In our view, those 
problems are solvable, but importantly they also open a window for incumbents 
to respond and adapt existing platforms/offerings to compete. 
So What Does This Mean for the Companies in Our Coverage?
• While among the most adversely impacted stocks last week, we see no clear 
negative implications for AppLovin from world models or other new game 
production technologies. The company is neither a game engine nor a game 
publisher (it divested those assets in '25) and should not see fundamental 
headwinds in either of our scenarios. AppLovin could arguably even benefit, 
if a proliferation of AI-generated games makes discovery more difficult and 
raises demand for user acquisition marketing. 
• Unity remains the most exposed to disruption from new game production 
tools. The Create engine is core to the company's value proposition 
(including the ad business) and Unity needs to build AI into every aspect of 
its platform to compete. That said, we believe the company is well 
positioned to do this, since the constraints around world models create an 
opportunity to execute. We are encouraged by its quick rollout of an AI 
assistant and inference engine in 2023, as well as the 2025 beta launch of

M
 Foundation
Morgan Stanley Research
5
Unity AI.
• As a content creation tool, Roblox is arguably positioned similarly to Unity. 
However, we see it as even more defensible, since its end-to-end game 
creation/distribution platform is far more than just a 3P game engine. That 
said, Roblox relies on lowering barriers to game creation and will need to 
build AI-driven automation into Roblox Studio to fend off competition. 
Fortunately for Roblox, we believe it already stands out as an AI adopter, 
with multiple tools (generative models, coding assistants etc.) available in 
Roblox Studio today...but also exciting advances in player-facing AI tools, 
which entered beta in 2025. 
• Take-Two maintains some proprietary game engines, which new technology 
could render obsolete. That said, we see Take-Two's core value proposition in 
its creative and intellectual property, not its tech. So while adopting new 
game products tools could be disruptive, we ultimately see Take-Two as a 
creative enterprise that can (and should) adopt new technology as it 
becomes available, with limited risk to doing so.
Exhibit 5:
We provide a framework to assess how different game ecosystem 
players could be impacted by AI-driven changes to how video games are 
produced. Notably, pure play mobile ad networks like APP do not appear in this 
framework as we see no clear read across from changes to the game 
development process. 
Source: Company Data, Morgan Stanley Research
New Tech Could Create An AI-Disruption Overhang, But We See Significant 
Opportunity Along with the Risk: To be clear, AI disruption narratives can weigh on 
multiples over long periods, as we have seen across Internet (e.g. GOOGL and ride 
share) as well as much of Software. The onus will be on APP, U, RBLX, and TTWO to 
articulate how they are deploying AI to drive engagement, monetization, and return 
on invested capital. That said, AI tools could also create entirely new opportunities

6
for the video game industry. The next generation of games may be built using AI, but 
they will also build it into the gameplay experience. We expect this to open new 
creative and business opportunities that the industry could also benefit from.

Source: GameNGen, id Software, Morgan Stanley Research
A New Approach to Game Creation?
• In a white paper published in 2024, 
Google Research and DeepMind 
reported results from an entirely new 
methodology of game production.
• By training a world model on videos of 
the game Doom, researchers were able 
to produce a real-time, interactive 
experience that simulated Doom at 20 
FPS by using a single TPU. 
• The neural model enabled real-time 
gameplay in an environment trained on 
hours of “watching” real humans play 
the original Doom. 
• While the experiences in Google’s 
Genie 3 do not demonstrate the 
structure and logic of a video game, 
they also point to power of these tools 
to generate interactive 3D environments
But research from Google Deepmind points to a more revolutionary path, where 
generative AI world models replace traditional game creation tools entirely
